candidate.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — therapeutic drug monitoring and interpretation of diagnostic/laboratory data
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — steady state and therapeutic drug monitoring
candidate.educational_objective: Relate elimination half-life to approximate steady-state timing while recognizing that therapeutic drug-monitoring sampling remains medication-specific.

options.A: Steady state is reached after exactly one half-life for essentially all medications
options.B: Steady state is commonly approached after about 4 to 5 half-lives, while the actual level timing and target remain drug-specific
options.C: Only intravenous medications require time to reach steady state
options.D: Any random level obtained after several doses is equivalent to a correctly timed therapeutic drug level

candidate.rationale: For medications following first-order kinetics with regular dosing, steady-state concentration is commonly approached after about 4 to 5 half-lives. This is a pharmacokinetic rule of thumb, not a universal sampling rule: renal/hepatic function, nonlinear kinetics, loading strategies, and medication-specific peak/trough protocols can alter when a level should be obtained and how it is interpreted. B is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Under common first-order conditions, steady state is approached after approximately 4–5 half-lives; drug kinetics and clinical context can create exceptions.
candidate.source_locator: Definition/Introduction — repeated regular dosing reaches steady-state concentration after approximately 4 to 5 half-lives; pharmacokinetic assumptions/caveats
candidate.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
candidate.stem: A medication follows approximately first-order pharmacokinetics, and its therapeutic level is ordinarily interpreted after steady state. Which principle is most accurate?
